beats.new_visual_element: Claude composer — the ask lands answered
beats.narration_text: Hey, this is Param Madan, and this explainer video is on why the physics engine never lets the A.I. do arithmetic. Here's a strange result. In one study, researchers gave an A.I. model the exact same addition problems, twice. The only change was adding commas to the numbers. Its accuracy jumped from about seventy-six percent to almost ninety-eight.

props.command: Why doesn't the physics engine let the AI do its own arithmetic?
output: AI models read numbers in chunks, not digits
So their arithmetic can shift with formatting
The engine hands every calculation to a solver

beats.narration_text: In the next few minutes you'll see three things. First, how an A.I. model actually sees a number, and why that's different from how you see it. Second, why that makes its arithmetic fragile, even when nothing random is going on. And third, what the physics engine does instead, and why it matters most when you're grading students. No math or coding background needed.

The answer, up front. A language model doesn't calculate. It predicts the next piece of text, one piece at a time. For arithmetic, that means the answer is a very good guess. Usually right, sometimes wrong, and hard to tell which. A calculator works the other way. It follows exact rules, so it's right every time. The physics engine gives the reading to the model, and every calculation to the calculator.

Here's why. A model doesn't read letter by letter, or digit by digit. It reads in chunks called tokens. The tokenizer used by G P T three point five and G P T four has a token for every number up to three digits. So a long number gets cut into three-digit chunks, starting from the left. Eight million, three hundred two thousand and eighty becomes eight-thirty, two-oh-eight, and zero. Notice those chunks don't line up with thousands at all.

When you add numbers by hand, you line them up from the right: ones, tens, hundreds. Left-to-right chunks break that alignment. So researchers at University College London and Google DeepMind tried a fix. They added commas, so the chunks start from the right instead, just like thousands. On seven to nine digit addition, G P T three point five went from seventy-five point six percent correct to ninety-seven point eight. Same problems. Different punctuation.

And here's the part that matters. In that study, randomness was switched off. The model gave its single most likely answer every time. So those mistakes weren't random slips. They were built into how the model sees numbers. The researchers also found the gap shrinks in bigger models. But smaller isn't zero, and better isn't the same as exact. A tutor that's right ninety-eight percent of the time is still wrong for some student, on some problem.

So the physics engine never asks the model for a number. The model's job is to read the problem and write down the knowns, the unknowns, and the units. Then SymPy, a symbolic math library, does the algebra and the arithmetic exactly, by rule, the way you would on paper. SymPy has no randomness in it at all. Give it the same equations and the same numbers, and it returns the same answer. The team's check runs one problem ten times, and gets identical output every time.

beats.new_visual_element: why exact matters for grading and hints
beats.narration_text: This matters most for grading. Two students who solve the same problem must be checked against the same correct answer, not whatever the model happened to produce that day. It helps tutoring too. The engine keeps equations as symbols until the very end, so a hint can show the relationship, tension minus mass times gravity equals mass times acceleration, instead of leaking a half-done number.

So here's the takeaway you can use today. When an A.I. gives you a number, ask whether it calculated it, or predicted it. If you need it to be right, ask it to write the calculation as code and run it, so a real calculator does the math. These percentages will change as models change. The rule won't. Let the model read. Let a calculator calculate.
Your turn. Paste this into Claude with any problem that has numbers in it. It asks Claude to do every calculation in code, and to show you what it ran.

props.command: Here is a problem: [paste it]. Do not do any arithmetic in your head. Write every calculation as code, run it, and show me the code and its output next to your explanation.

beats.narration_text: That's why the physics engine keeps the math away from the model. This has been Param Madan. Thanks for watching.
